messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Riemannian mc
parts: I understand this is already somewhat implemented in Stan, but not available due to limitations with the autodiff? Just wondering if there is any sort of expected time frame on this, or any way to make use of it as is? I think it would be helpful for the sorts of models I'm interested in. If it's still a long way away I might put a more concerted effort into getting a rough implementation of http://www2.warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/statistics/staff/academic-research/lan/publication/lmc.pdf , just to see how things go...

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Riemannian mc
parts:
On Nov 28, 2016, at 6:25 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:

I understand this is already somewhat implemented in Stan, but not available due to limitations with the autodiff?

Michael already implemented RHMC in the Stan (github.com/stan-dev/stan) code base. It has not been enabled in any of the interfaces for 2 good reasons related to higher order autodiff. 

1. For any expression in the Stan language, reverse mode autodiff works. That's what Stan currently needs. For forward mode autodiff, not only does everything not compile, we're uncertain about which functions have bugs. We could use help with both implementation and testing of higher order autodiff. 

2. Builds. It won't work on Windows using the g++ distributed with RTools. (It might with the latest version; I haven't checked in a while.) Builds will take something like 5x longer (don't quote me on time). And that's all conditional on #1.
Just wondering if there is any sort of expected time frame on this, or any way to make use of it as is?

If you're comfortable with C++, it's straightforward getting it working. Just a couple tweaks necessary. 

You're on your own for results, though. I don't think any of the dev team is ready to take on users pushing higher order autodiff when we know it's untested.
I think it would be helpful for the sorts of models I'm interested in.

Just curious: what makes you think that? Are gradients at different points of the lpdf in the typical set varying wildly? Are there any reparameterizations you can do? I think even recognizing that issue probably means you can do something to solve it.

If it's still a long way away I might put a more concerted effort into getting a rough implementation of http://www2.warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/statistics/staff/academic-research/lan/publication/lmc.pdf , just to see how things go...

--

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Riemannian mc
parts: Ok thanks for the details. I have the vague impression it might be helpful because there are strong colinearities between various parameters at certain regions of the space with certain data sets / priors. I'm undecided as to what would be more taxing for me - finding a way to properly understand these issues and then finding a way to reparameterise, or implement an algorithm someone else has written out. I've already thought about the former and the reparameterisations I did manage come with more compromises than I'd like :)  After thinking about the question though I think I should probably first try just with a dense metric, so, I might look at that code sometime in the next months, if the bugs are not already ironed out...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Riemannian mc
parts:
The co-linearities aren't a problem if the scales are similar.
The biggest issue that RHMC can overcome is if the curvature
varies dramatically, as in some hierarchical models.

And if the reparameterization comes with compromises, it's
not a reparameterization in the sense we're talking about. We
reparameterize to fit exactly the same models with a different
basis of parameters (e.g., you can reparameterize a lognormal variate
as an exponentiated normal variable [plus Jacobian if you give it
a distribution, which gets you back to the lognormal distribution]).

- Bob

I thought if the colinearities only occurred at certain values of certain parameters it would be an issue, but ok.

@ reparameterization - Ok, I was thinking reparameterize more like the centered / non centered distinction. There are probably still ways to improve things with the approach you suggest, though I have the vague, possibly totally wrong, intuition it won't be the bulk of possible improvement... Currently just about everything is sampled from a normal(0,1), with a range of transforms then setting bounds,scales, and priors for the parameters I'm actually interested in. Any suggestions for diagnostics I can use, or maybe articles that would inform such a diagnosis?
